newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Denktash tough as Cyprus talks resume in Swiss Alps.
newsitem.headline: Denktash tough as Cyprus talks resume in Swiss Alps.

text.p: Greek and Turkish Cypriot leaders resume U.N.-brokered talks in Switzerland on Monday in an effort to reunite their divided island, with both sides damping down optimism despite mounting pressure for a solution.

Glafcos Clerides and Rauf Denktash will negotiate for five days under a media blackout at a luxury hotel in the Swiss mountain resort of Glion near the city of Montreux following a first round of talks in Troutbeck, New York, last month.
Both sides are raising the stakes, with Cyprus preparing for entry talks with the European Union early next year and Turkey saying it will move towards partial integration with the north.

Denktash spoke negatively on prospects for a deal on the eve of the talks, accusing the world of ignoring the Turkish Cypriot position and the EU of getting in the way of an accord to reunite the island under a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.
In an interview with Reuters, he said he was prepared for the talks to break down rather than compromise on EU membership talks and the Turkish Cypriot demand of sovereign equality.
That is anathema to the Greek Cypriots who point out the Turkish Cypriots make up 18 percent of the island's population.

Denktash said: "We want the EU to understand that by interfering with the affairs of Cyprus at a very crucial stage, by giving a green light to one of the parties to represent the whole island and to become a member, it destroyed chances of a settlement."
"If the EU talks start, the intercommunal talks will stop and that will be the end of the matter," said Denktash.

"If the EU accession talks begin and we stop intercommunal talks, as we must, naturally we'll take the same steps vis-a-vis Turkey as the Greek Cypriot side will take vis-a-vis the EU. We have an alternative. We do not depend on a future solution."
Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain, when a government representing both communities broke apart amid violence.

They have been separated since 1974 when Turkey invaded the northern third of the island in response to a coup in the capital Nicosia backed by the junta then ruling Greece. Only Ankara recognises the Turkish Cypriot state proclaimed in 1983.

The New York meeting was the first in three years between the 73-year-old Denktash and 78-year-old Clerides, who have known -- and battled -- each other for nearly half a century, since both were young, London-trained lawyers.

In Glion, they will be joined by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan's special adviser for Cyprus, former Ecuadorean Foreign Minister Diego Cordovez, who helped negotiate the 1988 Geneva accords that led to the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan.
On the table is a U.N.-drafted document urging the two sides to commit themselves to a sustained process of direct talks.
A Greek Cypriot election campaign is expected to put a damper on further talks until after February's presidential vote.

"I do not know of anything of substance being discussed since Troutbeck," said a senior Greek Cypriot diplomat. "The U.N. wants to maintain a good climate before the end of the year. Real negotiations will be only after elections."
One source close to the talks described the Glion meeting as "keeping up the appearances".
If the latest round of talks fail, diplomats fear the east Mediterranean island could end up being more divided than ever.

Despite the island's 23-year-old partition, however, Cypriot proverbs is one thing the two communities still have in common. Mediators in Glion may find one of them particularly apt:: "Everyone pulls the quilt over to his side."
